name: AMDT AI Traffic Analytics
author: Juan Moyano Ecenarro

sections.description:
AMDT AI Traffic Analytics watches; it does not touch. It records two things your usual analytics do not show:

  • The AI bots that read your pages (GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot, Googlebot, Bingbot and the rest), and whether each one is who it says it is. It checks the bot’s IP address against the lists its operator publishes and against its reverse DNS, and flags as an impostor any visitor that uses another bot’s name. The Bot catalog shows how big each list is and the date its operator gave it, so you can tell a list kept up to date from one left untouched for a year. Agents that sign their requests with Web Bot Auth (Google-Agent, and ChatGPT agent, which uses the User-Agent of an ordinary Chrome) are verified by their signature, which cannot be forged the way a User-Agent can; IP analysis lists each signed visit with its three headers.
  • The people who arrive from an AI assistant (ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, Gemini, Copilot…) after clicking a citation, and the page they land on.

With that it gives you a dashboard (its chart of content consumption also as a panel of the WordPress Dashboard), a log you can filter and export, and an analysis of the addresses it could not identify, with blocking rules already written for Apache, Nginx, Cloudflare or Wordfence. You apply those rules in your firewall: the plugin does not block anyone.

It also publishes your site’s llms.txt (an index of your content for language models), counts who reads it, and lets you leave posts out of it from the editor.

And with Agent-Readiness it tells you whether an AI agent that navigates and acts on pages (it fills in forms, presses buttons, opens menus) can use yours. It reads the HTML your server gives for the home page, a sample post, up to 8 pages and a sample product, or for any page of your site you paste, and for each one:

  • scores from 0 to 100 what such an agent relies on: real buttons and links, the heading outline, the landmarks, labelled form fields, image alternatives and how much of the page is bare div;
  • approximates Lighthouse’s «Agentic Browsing» audits as far as the server can tell them: the 33 accessibility rules of its accessibility-tree audit, the WebMCP ones, llms.txt and the ARD manifest. Visual stability (CLS) needs a browser: each result links to PageSpeed Insights for it;
  • says how much of the text reaches the initial HTML and how much needs JavaScript;
  • explains how to fix it with your page builder (Elementor, Divi, Bricks, Beaver Builder, WPBakery, the block editor or your theme), and exports everything to Markdown or CSV.

It only analyses your own site, and it never changes your pages.

A complete edition, with more modules, also serves your content to AI agents through an API and an MCP server, publishes the files that announce them, declares AI usage permissions, protects that API and analyses your content. Both editions share the same tables and settings: you can move from one to the other without losing data.

What it stores

In your own database, for the retention you choose (30, 60 or 90 days):

  • For the bots in its catalogue and for whoever reads your llms.txt: the IP address, the User-Agent and the page requested.
  • For people who arrive from an AI assistant: only the network of their IP address (IPv4 up to the third block, IPv6 the first 48 bits), never the full address, plus the User-Agent, the page and the address of the assistant they came from.
  • For automated browsers that pretend to be an iPhone (possibly Grok): the request, with its IP address.
  • For requests signed with Web Bot Auth: also their three signature headers (Signature-Agent, Signature-Input, Signature) and the result of checking them.

Nothing is stored about ordinary visitors. If you turn on the debug log (Settings → Diagnostics), its entries also contain IP addresses and User-Agents. It is written to its own folder in uploads, amdt-ai-traffic-analytics/, in a file with a random key in its name; the folder denies direct access on servers that read .htaccess, such as Apache. It is deleted on uninstall if you choose to delete the data. Settings → Privacy → Policy guide has a suggested text for your privacy policy.

What it leaves in your visitors’ browsers

Nothing: no cookies, nothing stored in the browser. Pages carry a small script that, only when the visitor comes from an AI assistant, tells your own server about it.

External services

The plugin sends nothing to its author and has no telemetry. It connects to the services below. The IP lists and the signing keys are off on a new install until you turn them on.

Why the IP lists. To confirm that a visit from GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot, ChatGPT-User, OAI-AdsBot, ClaudeBot, Claude-User, Claude-SearchBot, PerplexityBot or Perplexity-User really comes from its operator, the plugin can download, once a day, the lists of IP addresses those operators publish. It is off until you turn it on: a notice asks you when you activate the plugin, and Settings has the switch.

What is sent, and when. Once a day while the switch is on, and once when you turn it on, the plugin makes a plain HTTPS GET request for each public file below. The request carries the plugin’s name and version as its user agent and nothing else: no data about your site, your visitors or you.

OpenAI (GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot, ChatGPT-User, OAI-AdsBot)

  • Files downloaded: https://openai.com/gptbot.json, https://openai.com/searchbot.json, https://openai.com/chatgpt-user.json, https://openai.com/adsbot.json
  • What they are: Overview of OpenAI Crawlers
  • Provided by OpenAI: terms of use, privacy policy

Anthropic (ClaudeBot, Claude-User, Claude-SearchBot)

  • File downloaded: https://claude.com/crawling/bots.json. claude.com is Anthropic’s domain for Claude; its own pages link Anthropic’s terms and privacy policy, below.
  • What it is: Does Anthropic crawl data from the web, and how can site owners block the crawler?
  • Provided by Anthropic: consumer terms, privacy policy, Anthropic Privacy Center

Perplexity (PerplexityBot, Perplexity-User)

  • Files downloaded: https://www.perplexity.ai/perplexitybot.json, https://www.perplexity.ai/perplexity-user.json. These are the addresses Perplexity’s documentation gives; until 2.7.13 the plugin used www.perplexity.com, which redirects to them.
  • What they are: Perplexity Crawlers
  • Provided by Perplexity: terms of service, privacy notice

Google and OpenAI (the keys of Google-Agent’s and ChatGPT agent’s signatures)

Google-Agent and ChatGPT agent sign some of their requests (Web Bot Auth, an IETF draft based on HTTP Message Signatures, RFC 9421). To check such a signature the plugin downloads the public keys of the agent that signed it. It does so only when a signed visit from one of them arrives and the keys it keeps are out of date (they are kept as long as the response allows, between five minutes and a day), only from the two addresses below, never from an address a visit names, and only while the switch of the IP lists is on (Settings → Operator IP lists). The request is a plain HTTPS GET with the plugin’s name and version as its user agent and nothing else.

  • Files downloaded: https://agent.bot.goog/.well-known/http-message-signatures-directory (Google-Agent), https://chatgpt.com/.well-known/http-message-signatures-directory (ChatGPT agent)
  • What they are: Authenticate requests with Web Bot Auth (experimental), ChatGPT agent allowlisting
  • Provided by Google: terms of service, privacy policy. Provided by OpenAI: terms of use, privacy policy

Reverse DNS

To tell which network a bot’s address belongs to, the plugin asks the DNS resolver your server uses for the name of the IP address of the bots and of whoever reads your llms.txt (never of the people who arrive from an assistant). This goes through your server’s own resolver, as any reverse lookup does. At most two lookups wait for an answer at the same time; a visit that finds both in use for more than 0.1 s is logged as unverified instead of waiting (the amdt_ait_rdns_max_concurrent filter changes the number, and 0 turns reverse DNS off).

Your own site

When you open the Dashboard or Settings, the plugin requests your own home page, at most twice a day, to find out whether a cache sits in front of WordPress, and your own /llms.txt, at most once a day, to check that visitors get it. Both are requests to your own server; the “Check again” buttons repeat them on demand.

When you run Agent-Readiness, the plugin requests the pages of your site it analyses and, for the Lighthouse audits, your site’s /llms.txt, /robots.txt and the addresses where an ARD manifest can be (/.well-known/ard.json, /.well-known/ai-catalog.json and any your pages announce). Only your own site, with its certificate checked; nothing else is contacted. The PageSpeed Insights link next to each result is an ordinary link: the plugin sends nothing to Google, and what PageSpeed Insights receives is what you send it if you open the link.

Third-party libraries

The charts of the plugin’s Dashboard, and its panel on the WordPress Dashboard, use Chart.js 4.6.1 (MIT license), bundled in admin/js/chart.umd.min.js: the minified build its authors publish on npm, without the line that points to its source map. Its source code: https://github.com/chartjs/Chart.js

The accessibility rules of Agent-Readiness use the WAI-ARIA tables of axe-core 4.14.0, Copyright (c) Deque Systems, Inc., under the Mozilla Public License 2.0, which is compatible with the GPL. They are in includes/data/aria-standards.php, generated from its lib/standards folder; the rules are written in PHP following its own, and the texts of each rule are based on its help texts. Its source code: https://github.com/dequelabs/axe-core
sections.installation:
1. Install the plugin from Plugins → Add New, or upload the amdt-ai-traffic-analytics folder to /wp-content/plugins/.
  2. Activate it.
  3. Decide whether to download the operators’ IP lists and signing keys (the notice after activation, or Settings). Without them, visits from OpenAI’s and Perplexity’s bots are logged as unverified, and signatures are kept unchecked.
  4. If a CDN or a proxy other than Cloudflare sits in front of your site, declare it in AI Traffic → Settings → Visitor IP. Otherwise every visit is logged with the proxy’s address.
  5. If you use a page cache plugin, see AI Traffic → Settings → Sync with cache plugins.
sections.faq:
Does it block bots?

No. It reports, and gives you the rule already written; deciding and applying it is up to you.

I use a cache plugin. Does it still measure?

Not entirely, and it is worth knowing: a page the cache serves without running WordPress does not go through the plugin, so that bot visit is not logged. With WP Rocket, LiteSpeed Cache or W3 Total Cache, Settings → Sync with cache plugins offers to keep bots out of the cache with one button, and tells you what it costs. With a server cache (nginx, Varnish, your host’s, Cloudflare caching HTML) or with WP Super Cache it cannot be done; the screen explains it when it detects one, which is not always. An agent that signs its requests but uses a browser’s User-Agent, such as ChatGPT agent, cannot be kept out of the cache that way: it is seen only on the pages the cache does not serve. Visits of people from AI assistants are measured on cached pages too: the browser reports them. If WP Rocket (Delay JavaScript execution) or LiteSpeed Cache (Load JS Deferred: Delayed) hold scripts back until the visitor touches the page, the plugin lets its own small script through, so a visitor who reads and leaves without scrolling is still counted. Other optimizers with a similar option have not been tested; if yours holds scripts back, exclude the one with the id amdt-ait-referral-tracker. The Dashboard also warns you when it finds a cache in front of WordPress, says where to act, and checks again when you ask it to.

What if Yoast SEO or Rank Math already serves my llms.txt?

Then that plugin serves it, and this one neither generates its own nor can count who reads it; the Dashboard says so.

Why are visits from GPTBot or PerplexityBot “unverified”?

Because the download of the operators’ IP lists is off. Turn it on in AI Traffic → Settings → Operator IP lists. ClaudeBot, Googlebot and Bingbot are still checked by reverse DNS without the lists.

Is the data deleted when I uninstall it?

Not by default. Only if you untick “Keep data on uninstall” in Settings, and never while the other edition is still installed.
sections.changelog:
2.7.24

  • Reverse DNS: at most two lookups wait for an answer at the same time. Each lookup runs inside the request of the visit being measured, so a burst of addresses never seen before, while DNS was slow, kept one PHP worker waiting per address for the resolver’s whole timeout, all at once; and a slow reverse zone behind a working resolver never triggered the ten-minute pause. Now a visit that finds both slots in use waits up to 0.1 s for one; if they are still in use, it is not looked up and is logged as unverified, never as an impostor. Nothing is cached, so the address is checked on its next visit. The slots are file locks in the server’s temporary folder, shared by every PHP worker and released even if one dies (MySQL’s GET_LOCK() where that folder cannot be used). The amdt_ait_rdns_max_concurrent filter changes the number; 0 turns reverse DNS off. Settings → Diagnostics shows the limit and in how many minutes a lookup found no free slot.
  • Reverse DNS: the check that a host name resolves back to the address is cached under the domain without its wildcard, so *.googlebot.com and googlebot.com no longer make one lookup each. A Googlebot visit from an unlisted address made 2 forward lookups, now 1; with five names in its PTR record, 9, now 5.
  • Load test (PHP-FPM with 10 workers; 50 simultaneous requests from new addresses with Googlebot’s User-Agent, with empty caches; a DNS server that does not answer, 5 s per lookup): with a slow reverse zone, p50 from 15.9 s to 0.93 s, p95 from 26.3 s to 1.54 s, and 50 DNS lookups down to 2; the time the workers spent inside PHP, from 262 s to 22 s. With the resolver down, p50 from 5.8 s to 0.98 s. Reading /llms.txt with Chrome’s User-Agent, p50 from 15.2 s to 0.56 s. With a DNS that answers, as before. Every visit was logged as unverified, none as an impostor.
  • Tested on the ZIPs of this version: every earlier battery, all passing, and 80 checks of this release on this edition: the limit and its filter; slots taken with files or, without the temporary folder, with database locks; waiting for a slot freed after 50 ms and giving up on one held for 0.4 s; no lookup and nothing cached without a slot; Diagnostics; and the lookups one Googlebot visit makes. 459 deliberate faults, all caught by the tests. Plugin Check 2.1.0: 0 errors (182 warnings). With every category, 0 errors (186 warnings), as in 2.7.23. With the settings WordPress.org uses on each upload, nothing. Correction to 2.7.23: «every earlier battery, all passing» was not so. Two checks of one battery looked for a Spanish heading as it read before the translation was revised («plugins de cache», now «de caché»); the plugin was right, and the test was corrected.
  • Thanks to PeepSo for reporting the slow reverse-DNS case.

2.7.23

  • llms.txt: when your SEO plugin (Yoast SEO, Rank Math or All in One SEO) marks a whole content type as noindex, its entries are no longer listed one by one to leave them out: the type is left out, or only its entries set to «index» are asked for. The file lists the same entries as before, sticky posts included. On a test site with 100,000 posts of a noindex type, each llms.txt took 335 ms instead of 68 ms and some 60 MB more memory; now it takes 7 ms and no more memory.
  • The plugin’s queries of noindex entries no longer set suppress_filters to true themselves. It is what get_posts() does by default, so nothing changes: entries in every language are still seen with WPML and Polylang. Plugin Check flagged it as an error under the WordPress VIP performance rules.
  • Spanish translation: the 206 strings the Spanish (Spain) team changed on translate.wordpress.org to follow its glossary, so that the translation bundled with the plugin says the same as the language pack. The checks cover the debug log’s folder, also on a real Apache 2.4, uninstall, the old action name, the settings’ callbacks, the notices, Chart.js and this readme.

2.7.10

  • No changes in this edition: 2.7.10 only changes the complete edition’s AIO analysis. Both editions carry the same version number.

2.7.9

2.7.8

  • llms.txt can say what your site is for: a new setting, “What the site is for”, one use per line (up to 8, of 200 characters each). It is published as a “When to use this site” section under the description. Left empty, as it comes, nothing is published: the plugin does not make it up. With WPML it is translated in String Translation. When an SEO plugin serves llms.txt, the section is added to its file.
  • WebMCP detections, which only the complete edition records, are no longer counted as consumption on the Dashboard, and the rows it wrote are relabelled from “(agéntico)” to “(WebMCP)” once, on update. In a site that only ever had this edition, nothing changes.
  • Tested on the ZIP of this version: the “When to use this site” section with and without text, WordPress’s redirects for every client, and Plugin Check 2.1.0 with 0 errors.

2.7.7

  • No changes in this edition: 2.7.7 only changes the complete edition’s MCP server, its WebMCP tools and its files for AI agents. Both editions carry the same version number.

2.7.6

  • llms.txt leaves out the entries your SEO plugin marks noindex: Yoast SEO, Rank Math and All in One SEO (the entry’s own setting, or else that of its content type and, in Rank Math and All in One SEO, the global one), and SEOPress (the entry’s setting). An SEO plugin counts only while it is active. WordPress’s “Discourage search engines” setting does not count.
  • The products section of llms.txt now respects the “Exclude from the AI surfaces” box, like the other sections.
  • The “AI access” box in the editor says when the SEO plugin already leaves the entry out.

2.7.4

The list comes with the plugin; no server is asked for it.
  • A notice when an operator’s agent that reads for people (ChatGPT-User, Claude-User, Perplexity-User…) stops reading while its search crawler keeps reading, after reading every week of the three before: the trace of a block on the way, such as Cloudflare’s new defaults. It says when the site seems to be behind Cloudflare, and it can be hidden for 7 days.

Google-Extended and Applebot-Extended are switched off and marked as robots.txt tokens: no crawler sends them. Applebot and OAI-AdsBot are added.
  • Visits from AI assistants: copilot.com, deepseek.com and meta.ai are added, and a visit without a Referer but with the utm_source=chatgpt.com that ChatGPT adds to its links counts as ChatGPT.

2.7.2

  • The notice about a cache in front of WordPress names the header that gives it away and says what to do in that case: Cloudflare keeping the HTML, the nginx cache of the hosting (with where Plesk turns it off), or another hosting or CDN cache. It has a “Check again” button: after that cache was turned off, the notice used to stay for up to 12 hours.
  • “More details in Settings” now goes to the panel of that cache.

2.7.1

  • Visits from AI assistants are counted even when WP Rocket (Delay JavaScript execution) or LiteSpeed Cache (Load JS Deferred: Delayed) hold scripts back until the visitor touches the page: the plugin lets its own small script through, and nothing else of theirs is touched.

  • First public release.

short_description: See which AI bots crawl your site, whether they are who they claim to be, and who arrives from ChatGPT, Claude or Perplexity. Publishes llms.txt.
description:
AMDT AI Traffic Analytics watches; it does not touch. It records two things your usual analytics do not show:

  • The AI bots that read your pages (GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot, Googlebot, Bingbot and the rest), and whether each one is who it says it is. It checks the bot’s IP address against the lists its operator publishes and against its reverse DNS, and flags as an impostor any visitor that uses another bot’s name. The Bot catalog shows how big each list is and the date its operator gave it, so you can tell a list kept up to date from one left untouched for a year. Agents that sign their requests with Web Bot Auth (Google-Agent, and ChatGPT agent, which uses the User-Agent of an ordinary Chrome) are verified by their signature, which cannot be forged the way a User-Agent can; IP analysis lists each signed visit with its three headers.
  • The people who arrive from an AI assistant (ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, Gemini, Copilot…) after clicking a citation, and the page they land on.

With that it gives you a dashboard (its chart of content consumption also as a panel of the WordPress Dashboard), a log you can filter and export, and an analysis of the addresses it could not identify, with blocking rules already written for Apache, Nginx, Cloudflare or Wordfence. You apply those rules in your firewall: the plugin does not block anyone.

It also publishes your site’s llms.txt (an index of your content for language models), counts who reads it, and lets you leave posts out of it from the editor.

And with Agent-Readiness it tells you whether an AI agent that navigates and acts on pages (it fills in forms, presses buttons, opens menus) can use yours. It reads the HTML your server gives for the home page, a sample post, up to 8 pages and a sample product, or for any page of your site you paste, and for each one:

  • scores from 0 to 100 what such an agent relies on: real buttons and links, the heading outline, the landmarks, labelled form fields, image alternatives and how much of the page is bare div;
  • approximates Lighthouse’s «Agentic Browsing» audits as far as the server can tell them: the 33 accessibility rules of its accessibility-tree audit, the WebMCP ones, llms.txt and the ARD manifest. Visual stability (CLS) needs a browser: each result links to PageSpeed Insights for it;
  • says how much of the text reaches the initial HTML and how much needs JavaScript;
  • explains how to fix it with your page builder (Elementor, Divi, Bricks, Beaver Builder, WPBakery, the block editor or your theme), and exports everything to Markdown or CSV.

It only analyses your own site, and it never changes your pages.

A complete edition, with more modules, also serves your content to AI agents through an API and an MCP server, publishes the files that announce them, declares AI usage permissions, protects that API and analyses your content. Both editions share the same tables and settings: you can move from one to the other without losing data.

What it stores

In your own database, for the retention you choose (30, 60 or 90 days):

  • For the bots in its catalogue and for whoever reads your llms.txt: the IP address, the User-Agent and the page requested.
  • For people who arrive from an AI assistant: only the network of their IP address (IPv4 up to the third block, IPv6 the first 48 bits), never the full address, plus the User-Agent, the page and the address of the assistant they came from.
  • For automated browsers that pretend to be an iPhone (possibly Grok): the request, with its IP address.
  • For requests signed with Web Bot Auth: also their three signature headers (Signature-Agent, Signature-Input, Signature) and the result of checking them.

Nothing is stored about ordinary visitors. If you turn on the debug log (Settings → Diagnostics), its entries also contain IP addresses and User-Agents. It is written to its own folder in uploads, amdt-ai-traffic-analytics/, in a file with a random key in its name; the folder denies direct access on servers that read .htaccess, such as Apache. It is deleted on uninstall if you choose to delete the data. Settings → Privacy → Policy guide has a suggested text for your privacy policy.

What it leaves in your visitors’ browsers

Nothing: no cookies, nothing stored in the browser. Pages carry a small script that, only when the visitor comes from an AI assistant, tells your own server about it.

External services

The plugin sends nothing to its author and has no telemetry. It connects to the services below. The IP lists and the signing keys are off on a new install until you turn them on.

Why the IP lists. To confirm that a visit from GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot, ChatGPT-User, OAI-AdsBot, ClaudeBot, Claude-User, Claude-SearchBot, PerplexityBot or Perplexity-User really comes from its operator, the plugin can download, once a day, the lists of IP addresses those operators publish. It is off until you turn it on: a notice asks you when you activate the plugin, and Settings has the switch.

What is sent, and when. Once a day while the switch is on, and once when you turn it on, the plugin makes a plain HTTPS GET request for each public file below. The request carries the plugin’s name and version as its user agent and nothing else: no data about your site, your visitors or you.

OpenAI (GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot, ChatGPT-User, OAI-AdsBot)

  • Files downloaded: https://openai.com/gptbot.json, https://openai.com/searchbot.json, https://openai.com/chatgpt-user.json, https://openai.com/adsbot.json
  • What they are: Overview of OpenAI Crawlers
  • Provided by OpenAI: terms of use, privacy policy

Anthropic (ClaudeBot, Claude-User, Claude-SearchBot)

  • File downloaded: https://claude.com/crawling/bots.json. claude.com is Anthropic’s domain for Claude; its own pages link Anthropic’s terms and privacy policy, below.
  • What it is: Does Anthropic crawl data from the web, and how can site owners block the crawler?
  • Provided by Anthropic: consumer terms, privacy policy, Anthropic Privacy Center

Perplexity (PerplexityBot, Perplexity-User)

  • Files downloaded: https://www.perplexity.ai/perplexitybot.json, https://www.perplexity.ai/perplexity-user.json. These are the addresses Perplexity’s documentation gives; until 2.7.13 the plugin used www.perplexity.com, which redirects to them.
  • What they are: Perplexity Crawlers
  • Provided by Perplexity: terms of service, privacy notice

Google and OpenAI (the keys of Google-Agent’s and ChatGPT agent’s signatures)

Google-Agent and ChatGPT agent sign some of their requests (Web Bot Auth, an IETF draft based on HTTP Message Signatures, RFC 9421). To check such a signature the plugin downloads the public keys of the agent that signed it. It does so only when a signed visit from one of them arrives and the keys it keeps are out of date (they are kept as long as the response allows, between five minutes and a day), only from the two addresses below, never from an address a visit names, and only while the switch of the IP lists is on (Settings → Operator IP lists). The request is a plain HTTPS GET with the plugin’s name and version as its user agent and nothing else.

  • Files downloaded: https://agent.bot.goog/.well-known/http-message-signatures-directory (Google-Agent), https://chatgpt.com/.well-known/http-message-signatures-directory (ChatGPT agent)
  • What they are: Authenticate requests with Web Bot Auth (experimental), ChatGPT agent allowlisting
  • Provided by Google: terms of service, privacy policy. Provided by OpenAI: terms of use, privacy policy

Reverse DNS

To tell which network a bot’s address belongs to, the plugin asks the DNS resolver your server uses for the name of the IP address of the bots and of whoever reads your llms.txt (never of the people who arrive from an assistant). This goes through your server’s own resolver, as any reverse lookup does. At most two lookups wait for an answer at the same time; a visit that finds both in use for more than 0.1 s is logged as unverified instead of waiting (the amdt_ait_rdns_max_concurrent filter changes the number, and 0 turns reverse DNS off).

Your own site

When you open the Dashboard or Settings, the plugin requests your own home page, at most twice a day, to find out whether a cache sits in front of WordPress, and your own /llms.txt, at most once a day, to check that visitors get it. Both are requests to your own server; the “Check again” buttons repeat them on demand.

When you run Agent-Readiness, the plugin requests the pages of your site it analyses and, for the Lighthouse audits, your site’s /llms.txt, /robots.txt and the addresses where an ARD manifest can be (/.well-known/ard.json, /.well-known/ai-catalog.json and any your pages announce). Only your own site, with its certificate checked; nothing else is contacted. The PageSpeed Insights link next to each result is an ordinary link: the plugin sends nothing to Google, and what PageSpeed Insights receives is what you send it if you open the link.

Third-party libraries

The charts of the plugin’s Dashboard, and its panel on the WordPress Dashboard, use Chart.js 4.6.1 (MIT license), bundled in admin/js/chart.umd.min.js: the minified build its authors publish on npm, without the line that points to its source map. Its source code: https://github.com/chartjs/Chart.js

The accessibility rules of Agent-Readiness use the WAI-ARIA tables of axe-core 4.14.0, Copyright (c) Deque Systems, Inc., under the Mozilla Public License 2.0, which is compatible with the GPL. They are in includes/data/aria-standards.php, generated from its lib/standards folder; the rules are written in PHP following its own, and the texts of each rule are based on its help texts. Its source code: https://github.com/dequelabs/axe-core

screenshots.caption: Dashboard: visits of AI bots by bot and by day, how many were verified, and the people who arrived from an AI assistant.
Logs: every recorded visit, filtered by type, bot or date, with its verification result. Exportable to CSV.

IP analysis: how much of the traffic has a verified identity (by its address or by its Web Bot Auth signature), the signed requests with their headers, the operators behind it, and blocking rules ready for your firewall.
Bot catalog: the bots it recognises, who operates each one, how it is verified, and the size and date of each operator's IP list.
Settings: what is tracked, the download of the operators' IP lists and signing keys, and the visits from AI assistants.

Agent-Readiness: whether an AI agent can navigate and act on your pages, each template with its score, Lighthouse's Agentic Browsing audits as far as the server can tell them, and how to fix it with your page builder.
The WordPress Dashboard: the plugin's panel with the chart of content consumption, and the period each user chooses.
